newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein starts talks with British officials.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein starts talks with British officials.

text.p: Leading Sinn Fein representatives held their first talks with British officials on Monday since a week-old truce declared by their IRA guerrilla allies opened the door to official contact with governments.
Sinn Fein's vice-president, Pat Doherty, and other senior party officials arrived at Belfast's Stormont buildings to meet British government officials steering multi-party peace talks.
The Sinn Fein delegation also planned to meet former U.S. senator George Mitchell, who is chairing the slow-moving negotiations between pro-British unionists and Irish nationalists.
Monday's talks will be the first between Sinn Fein and the British government since the Irish Republican Army (IRA) called a new halt to its war against British rule of Northern Ireland one week ago.
The "unequivocal cessation" was greeted by the British and Irish governments with a lifting of a ban imposed after the IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February last year.
Sinn Fein's president, Gerry Adams, met Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern last Friday and said at the weekend that he expected to travel to the United States for top-level contacts in September.
But Sinn Fein will not be admitted to substantive negotiations which are due to start on September 15 until Britain is satisfied that the IRA truce is genuine.

To date there have been no IRA attacks although British security forces and the armed 12,000-strong Northern Ireland police remain on the alert against violence by Irish republicans or their Protestant pro-British loyalist foes.
Army "spy in the sky" helicopters still hover over the city by day and night and police still patrol in armoured jeeps, fully armed and wearing flak jackets.

Two Protestant unionist parties have walked out of the talks in protest against Britain's refusal to demand that Sinn Fein get the IRA to surrender its weapons as a condition for entry to the negotiations.

But the biggest unionist group, the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) of David Trimble, says it will stay in the negotiations but wants the ground rules changed to force an IRA arms surrender during the negotiations.

All three unionist parties voted against Anglo-Irish plans to seek "parallel decommissioning" of IRA arms during the negotiations, centrepiece of year-long efforts to lure the IRA to call a truce and get Sinn Fein involved in negotiations.
The vote, which torpedoed the plan, will be discussed when Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, and Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke meet in Dublin on Tuesday.
The UUP says the wording of the plan was too vague and wants it toughened to force the IRA to hand over weapons to prove that its war for a united Ireland is over for good.
The two governments say they are determined to press ahead with substantive talks in September but have to find a new compromise on arms surrender.
Adams said in a weekend interview that the IRA would never agree to the UUP's demand that it start handing over guns during or before the negotiations.
"There's no possibility -- and the IRA have made this very clear -- of them surrendering their weapons," he told Fox news.
